paragraphs.heading: Who he was
paragraphs.text: Justinian I, also called Justinian the Great, ruled the Roman Empire from 527 until 565. He is counted among the most prominent and influential Roman emperors. His reign is linked with a lasting law code, a burst of Byzantine culture and the building of Hagia Sophia.

paragraphs.heading: From peasant boy to heir
paragraphs.text: He came from a peasant family and grew up speaking Latin, one of the last Eastern Roman emperors to do so. His uncle Justin, who commanded a unit of the imperial guard, adopted him, brought him to Constantinople and saw that he was well taught in law, theology and Roman history. When the emperor Anastasius died in 518, Justinian helped Justin become emperor. As Justin grew senile, Justinian ran the empire in practice, and in 527 he was crowned co-emperor and then became sole ruler after Justin died that August.

paragraphs.heading: The emperor who never sleeps
paragraphs.text: Justinian worked so hard that he earned the nickname "the emperor who never sleeps", yet he seems to have been friendly and easy to approach. Around 525 he married Theodora, a former actress some twenty years younger than him. A law change by Justin had made such a marriage possible, and although it caused a scandal, Theodora became a powerful figure in imperial politics. She was said to match his energy and intelligence.

paragraphs.heading: Winning back the West
paragraphs.text: His great aim was renovatio imperii, the "restoration of the Empire", and it was only partly achieved. His general Belisarius quickly conquered the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa. Belisarius, Narses and others then took the Ostrogothic Kingdom, bringing Italy, Sicily, Dalmatia and Rome back into the empire. The praetorian prefect Liberius won back the south of the Iberian Peninsula, and together these wars restored Roman control of the western Mediterranean and added over a million solidi to yearly revenue.

paragraphs.heading: A law code that outlived him
paragraphs.text: One of his most lasting works was a uniform rewriting of Roman law, the Corpus Juris Civilis. It was used first across the Eastern Mediterranean. Today it still underlies the civil law of many modern states.

paragraphs.heading: Troubles at home
paragraphs.text: Not everyone loved his rule. Early on he almost lost his throne in the Nika riots, and as late as 562 a plot against his life was uncovered. His reign was also marked by religious quarrels between Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Christians. He caught the plague in the early 540s and survived, and he lived nearly twenty years after Theodora died in 548.
